title: Why Your Humor Isn't Working In Your Classroom
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin addresses teachers who feel their attempts at humor fall flat, arguing the problem isn't a lack of natural wit but three common mistakes. First, trying too hard to be funny undermines spontaneity and authentic personality. Second, planning jokes or rehearsing stories in advance rarely works, since even professional comedians need extensive practice to make planned material feel natural, time teachers don't have. Third, trying to be someone else—cooler, more relatable, using student slang—reads as inauthentic and undermines rapport rather than building it. His remedy for all three is rooted in improvisational comedy's core principle: stop trying to be funny and simply stay present, aware, and authentically yourself, trusting that humor arises naturally from attentiveness rather than effort. He closes by urging teachers to focus on enjoying their students rather than pursuing laughs directly.
points: Struggling with classroom humor is rarely about a lack of wit—it's usually one of three fixable mistakes.
Trying too hard to be funny undermines spontaneity, timing, and authentic personality.
Planning or rehearsing jokes rarely works in the classroom, since even professional comedians need extensive practice to appear natural.
Attempting to be "cool" or relatable by adopting student slang or attitudes reads as inauthentic and damages rapport.
The core fix, borrowed from improvisational comedy, is to stop trying to be funny and instead stay present and authentically oneself.
quotes: If you care too much and overthink it, you’ll lose your spontaneity. You’ll lose your timing and playfulness, your cleverness and quirkiness.
A classroom is a target-rich environment and by simply being aware and open-minded, what to say or do at the right moment will come to you without conscious thought.
But even professional comedians have to spend months, sometimes years, on their material, working out the perfect timing, pacing, and word choice just to get a reliable laugh.
When you try to be cool or speak to students on their level, using their lingo, attitudes, or sensibilities, it never works.
One of the tenets of improvisational comedy, which is the true secret to bringing more humor to your classroom, is to not try to be funny.
Just focus on enjoying your students and the laughs, the easy rapport, the likability, the love of being in your class . . . Will happen naturally.
